title: A Disguise That Fooled No One
overview: Jeroboam's sick son leads to a grim message about the end of his family, while in the south Rehoboam's Judah also turns to other gods and is plundered by Egypt.

parts.label: A mother in disguise (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: With his son gravely ill, Jeroboam sends his wife in disguise to Ahijah, the prophet who once promised him the throne, probably so no one would know he had turned to the LORD's prophet instead of his own new shrines. Her simple gifts suited a country woman, but the blind prophet, warned by God, names her the moment he hears her at the door.

parts.label: Judgment on Jeroboam's family (vv. 7-11)
parts.note: God reminds Jeroboam that he was raised from ordinary life to be king, yet he made metal idols, the golden calves of chapter 12, and led the nation away. The punishment is stark: every male of his line will be wiped out and their bodies left for dogs and birds, which was the worst disgrace in that world.

parts.label: The boy and the nation (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: The boy will die, but he alone of the family will be mourned and buried, because something good was found in him, though the text never says what. The prophet adds that a new king will end Jeroboam's line and that Israel itself will one day be uprooted and scattered beyond the Euphrates River for worshiping at Asherah poles, wooden poles honoring a Canaanite goddess.

parts.label: It happens as foretold (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: The boy dies the moment his mother steps into their house in Tirzah, Jeroboam's capital, and the whole nation mourns him as Ahijah said. Jeroboam reigns 22 years, his son Nadab follows him, and the fuller royal records mentioned here are now lost.

parts.label: Rehoboam's Judah goes astray (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: In the south, Solomon's son Rehoboam rules from Jerusalem, and his Ammonite mother is likely mentioned to hint at foreign religious influence. Judah fills the land with hilltop shrines, sacred stones, Asherah poles and what the text calls shrine prostitution, and the writer judges it worse than anything before.

parts.label: Gold becomes bronze (vv. 25-31)
parts.note: Shishak, most likely the pharaoh Sheshonq I, whose own inscriptions record a campaign into the region, raids Jerusalem and carries off the temple and palace treasures, including Solomon's gold shields. Rehoboam's bronze replacements are often read as a sign of how far the kingdom's glory had faded, and the war with the north never stops.

think: Jeroboam wanted an answer about his son without facing the prophet as himself; why might people seek help while hoping to stay hidden?
